title: Climacteric and non-climacteric produce — ethylene behaviour
text:
Bananas, avocados and tomatoes are climacteric fruits: as they ripen they show a strong peak in respiration with high internal ethylene production, and they respond to exogenous ethylene, which speeds softening and ripening.

Strawberries are non-climacteric: respiration stays roughly constant or declines until senescence, with little or no increase in internal ethylene production. (USDA AMS National Organic Program, Ethylene — Handling Technical Report, 2023.)

title: Hass Avocado — ethylene class
text: Hass Avocado is an ethylene producer — it can speed ripening and yellowing of ethylene-sensitive items stored or boxed with it.  Source: USDA AMS National Organic Program, 'Ethylene — Handling' Technical Report (2023), lines 177-183: bananas, avocado and tomato listed as climacteric; strawberry listed as non-climacteric with 'little or no increase in internal ethylene production'. https://www.ams.usda.gov/sites/default/files/media/2023Technical_Report_Ethylene_Handling.pdf

title: Retail waste and CO2e — avocados
text: FAO (2011) estimates that 12.0% of fruits and vegetables entering supermarket retail in North America and Oceania is lost or wasted there. Producing one kilogram emits about 1.05 kg CO2e (Poore & Nemecek 2018, 'Other Fruit (proxy; avocado not itemised)').

title: Avocados — storage
text: Avocados: store in the refrigerator for 3–4 days. Timeline for refrigerator applies to ripe fruit.

title: Bananas — storage
text: Bananas: store in the refrigerator for 3–3 days. Timeline for refrigerator applies to ripe fruit; skin will blacken.

title: Milk — plain or flavored — storage
text: Milk — plain or flavored: storage time: Package use-by date.

title: Fatty fish — bluefish, catfish, mackerel, mullet, salmon, tuna, etc. — storage
text: Fatty fish — bluefish, catfish, mackerel, mullet, salmon, tuna, etc.: store in the refrigerator for 1–2 days from the date of purchase.

title: Bread — homemade — storage
text: Bread — homemade: store in the pantry for 3–5 days. May have shorter shelf life due to lack of preservatives.

title: Bagged greens — leaf, spinach, lettuce, etc. — storage
text: Bagged greens — leaf, spinach, lettuce, etc.: store in the refrigerator for 3–5 days. Unopened product will last 3 - 5 days after date on bag; after opening it will last 2 days.

title: Strawberries — storage
text: Strawberries: store in the refrigerator for 2–3 days from the date of purchase.

title: Cherry tomatoes — storage
text: Cherry tomatoes: store in the pantry for 10–10 days.

title: How humidity speeds spoilage in the simulation
text: ShelfSense models ambient stress as an environment factor beta_env = 1 + 0.5 × clamp((RH − 50) / 50, 0, 1), so relative humidity above 50 % ages exposed products up to 1.5× faster. Each product's weather_exposure (0–1) scales how much of that stress reaches it: berries, bananas, avocados and tomatoes are fully exposed; spinach 0.8, bread 0.6, chilled salmon and milk 0.2.

title: How humidity speeds spoilage in the simulation
text: During a heavy rainstorm humidity jumps toward 98 % for 12 hours, then eases back over 6 hours. This is a modelling assumption for the demo, not a measured coefficient.

title: Spinach — postharvest handling and ethylene
text: Spinach is highly sensitive to exogenous ethylene: even low ethylene levels during distribution and short-term storage cause accelerated yellowing. Do not store or display spinach together with ethylene-producing items such as apples, melons and tomatoes.

title: Spinach — postharvest handling and ethylene
text: Wilting, yellowing of leaves and decay increase with storage time, and faster at common distribution temperatures of 5–10 °C; the optimum storage temperature is 0 °C. (Suslow, T. & Cantwell, M., Spinach: Recommendations for Maintaining Postharvest Quality.)
